title: Finding Outliers with IQR Fences
body:
When a dataset has a wild value that does not fit, a box plot uses fences to spot it. We look at the middle spread of the numbers, called the interquartile range, to draw these secret lines.

Look at the box plot to see where the fences sit compared to the extreme point.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Box plot with fences for data 3 to 40","caption":"IQR is $11.5-5.5=6$. Fences at $1.5 \\times \\mathrm{IQR}$ flag $40$ as an outlier.","kind":"box-plot","x":{"label":"Values","min":-5,"max":45},"boxes":[{"label":"Data distribution","values":[3,5,6,7,8,9,11,12,40],"whiskerLow":3,"q1":5.5,"median":8,"q3":11.5,"whiskerHigh":12,"fences":{"lower":-3.5,"upper":20.5},"outliers":[{"label":"Extreme value","value":40}]}]}}
```

For the sorted data 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 40, the first quartile is 5.5 and the third quartile is 11.5. The interquartile range is the gap between them, which is 6.

Fences are placed $1.5$ times this range beyond the quartiles. This creates an upper fence at $11.5 + 9 = 20.5$ and a lower fence at $5.5 - 9 = -3.5$.

Any data point lying past these fences, such as 40, is flagged as an outlier.

title: Exam Scores Box Plot
body:
When teachers want to see how a class did, they often look at the middle score and the spread. For these ten exam scores, half the class scored below 68.5 and half scored above it.

Look at the box in the plot below to see where the middle half of the students scored, stretching from 61 to 75 points.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Exam scores with an outlier","caption":"The interquartile range is 14, making the upper fence 96. The score 98 sits past this fence as an outlier.","kind":"box-plot","x":{"label":"Score","min":40,"max":110,"unit":"points"},"boxes":[{"label":"Exam scores","values":[52,55,61,64,67,70,72,75,78,98],"whiskerLow":52,"q1":61,"median":68.5,"q3":75,"whiskerHigh":78,"fences":{"lower":40,"upper":96},"outliers":[{"label":"Outlier","value":98}]}]}}
```

Scores that fall way outside the main group are called outliers because they do not fit the usual pattern. Here, the score of 98 is far above the rest and sits past the upper fence limit.

Any score higher than 96 is flagged as an outlier in this data set, which makes 98 the single unusual value.

body:
A box plot summarizes data using five key numbers to show where values cluster. For our delivery times, the values are 12, 15, 17, 18, 20, 22, 24, 25, and 60 minutes.


Look at the central box in the plot, which spans from the first quartile at 16 to the third quartile at 24.5. This box shows the middle half of all delivery times.

The thick line inside the box marks the median delivery time of 20 minutes.

The whiskers extend out to the lowest and highest regular values, which are 12 and 25 minutes. Any value far away from the rest, like our 60-minute delivery, is marked separately as an outlier.

title: The 1.5 x IQR Rule for Response Times
body:
When a few server response times are much slower than the rest, standard charts get distorted. The interquartile range helps spot these unusual values by focusing on the middle half of the data.

Look at the box plot to see how the middle fifty percent sits between 87.5 ms and 107 ms. The span between them is the interquartile range, or IQR, which measures the spread of typical values.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Response times with outlier","caption":"IQR is 19.5. The upper fence at 136.25 marks the 300 ms value as an outlier.","kind":"box-plot","x":{"label":"Time","min":50,"max":320,"unit":"ms"},"boxes":[{"label":"Response times","values":[80,85,90,92,95,99,104,110,300],"whiskerLow":80,"q1":87.5,"median":95,"q3":107,"whiskerHigh":110,"fences":{"lower":58.25,"upper":136.25},"outliers":[{"label":"Lag spike","value":300}]}]}}
```

The rule multiplies this IQR span by 1.5 and adds it above the upper quartile to set a boundary called a fence.

Any data point sitting beyond this fence is marked separately as an outlier rather than stretching the main whiskers.

title: Finding Outliers With The IQR Rule
body:
When a website takes too long to load, we measure response times in milliseconds to check performance. Most requests finish quickly, but a single very slow request can distort the average.

A box plot helps us see the spread of these times without letting extreme values hide the pattern.

Look at the box plot to see how the middle fifty percent of response times cluster together, while the extreme value stands apart.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Response times with outlier","caption":"IQR is 19.5. Q1 is 87.5, Q3 is 107. Lower fence is 58.25, upper fence is 136.25. The value 300 ms is an outlier.","kind":"box-plot","x":{"label":"Time (ms)","min":50,"max":320,"unit":"ms"},"boxes":[{"label":"Response times","values":[80,85,90,92,95,99,104,110,300],"whiskerLow":80,"q1":87.5,"median":95,"q3":107,"whiskerHigh":110,"fences":{"lower":58.25,"upper":136.25},"outliers":[{"label":"Slow request","value":300}]}]}}
```

The box spans from the first quartile to the third quartile, marking the middle of the data.

The $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ rule calculates fences to decide if a high value is a true outlier rather than just a normal fluctuation.

prompt: What does the 1.5 x IQR rule do to a box plot of response times 80, 85, 90, 92, 95, 99, 104, 110, 300 ms?
title: Finding Outliers With the 1.5 x IQR Rule
body:
When you have a set of response times like 80, 85, 90, 92, 95, 99, 104, 110, and 300 milliseconds, some values are normal while others are extreme spikes.

To find which ones are unusual, we use the interquartile range, which is the span between the middle of the lower half and the middle of the upper half.

Look at the box plot to see how the middle half sits alongside the single extreme spike at the right edge.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Response times with fences and outlier","caption":"IQR is $104 - 90 = 14$. The upper fence is $104 + 1.5 \\times 14 = 125$. The value 300 ms is an outlier.","kind":"box-plot","x":{"label":"Time (ms)","min":70,"max":320,"unit":"ms"},"boxes":[{"label":"Response times","values":[80,85,90,92,95,99,104,110,300],"whiskerLow":80,"q1":87.5,"median":95,"q3":107,"whiskerHigh":110,"fences":{"lower":58.25,"upper":136.25},"outliers":[{"label":"Spike","value":300}]}]}}
```

Multiplying that middle span by 1.5 gives us a boundary called a fence, beyond which any value is counted as an outlier.

Here, the upper fence lands at 125 milliseconds, so the 300 millisecond time sits far past it as a distinct point.
